items.title: Percy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: A.T. was there. And when his mother would go to work, we’d go to his house and practice for these gigs.

ctx.x: Yes, wow. What about Art Taylor? Was he around?

A.T. was there. And when his mother would go to work, we’d go to his house and practice for these gigs. We had these twelve dollar, ten dollar dance gigs around up in Harlem and a place down in Midtown, the name will come to me. Where they used to have, City Center, they used to have some dances in there. Those were the gigs I could take, and Miles gave me a gig and Birdland, I think it was January 1950, with Miles, Fats, Navarro, Bud Powell, Buhaina, Art Blakey and myself, sometimes we were in there a few weeks…

items.title: Percy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Arthur Taylor used to sit around all day with Max Roach records trying to play what Max Roach was playing.

ctx.x: Okay, stop that for a minute because that is a very significant point. What was the reason why he quit? Again, there are so many different versions of why he left. He was either kicked out or he wanted to leave…

No, he wasn’t kicked out. He just didn’t wanna do all that rehearsing and playing drum parts. Kenny did not want to play that kind of music. He was an innovator on his own as far as his instrument was concerned. He started [a] certain concept of punctuating. If you hear that thing that we did before the Modern Jazz Quartet, we were on a thing at Carnegie Hall with Charlie Parker, there’s a record out of that with Kenny and myself and John Lewis, and you can hear Kenny in the back, “Go Bird! That kind of bebop.”…

four things going along at the same time, we could not un-swing it, we couldn’t do it. Even the transcriptions, like I said before, the exact notations, the feeling had to be there, which it was. I imagine that was why we were successful for so long a period of time.
